group.passage:
In 1843, a young mathematician suggested that a machine might one day compose music. What makes her idea remarkable is that the machine she had in mind existed only on paper.
Ada Lovelace, born in 1815, was the poet Lord Byron’s only child. Her mother had her taught mathematics and science, partly in the hope of keeping her away from the poetic side of her father. Lovelace never attended a school or university, but she studied hard from childhood and later took a mathematics course by letter with Augustus De Morgan. Even so, the poet’s daughter did not give up imagination; she called her own way of thinking “poetical science.”
Her chance came through Charles Babbage, who from the mid-1830s had been designing a calculating machine called the Analytical Engine. It was to be controlled by punched cards, like those that guided the patterns on Jacquard weaving looms. In 1842, the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea published an account of the engine in French, and Lovelace was asked to translate it into English. Babbage suggested that she add notes of her own. When the paper appeared in 1843, signed only with her initials, her notes filled 41 of its 66 pages. The last of them, Note G, showed how the engine could calculate a series known as the Bernoulli numbers, and its table is often called the first computer program.
Yet her boldest idea had little to do with arithmetic. Babbage saw his engine mainly as a machine for numbers, but Lovelace noticed that the cards which told it what to do were separate from the values it worked on. In principle, then, it could handle anything that obeyed mathematical rules. If the relations between musical sounds could be expressed in such a form, she reasoned, the engine might compose pieces of any length and complexity.
She was careful not to claim too much, however. The engine, she wrote, could not originate anything; it could only carry out what people knew how to order it to do. Alan Turing later challenged this view, which he called “Lady Lovelace’s objection.” The engine itself was never built, but in 2015, at events in Oxford marking 200 years since her birth, a computer simulation of it produced a sequence of numbers that was then turned into a musical theme.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?

options.A: How Lovelace’s mother tried to keep her daughter away from poetry.
options.B: How Lovelace saw uses for a calculating machine that went beyond numbers.
options.C: How Lovelace and Babbage built the first machine that could compose music.
options.D: How the first computer program came to be written for the Bernoulli numbers.

questions.stem: Which of the following questions can be answered from the passage?

options.A: Who first asked Lovelace to translate Menabrea’s article?
options.B: Why was the Analytical Engine never built?
options.C: In what year did Alan Turing write about Lady Lovelace’s objection?
options.D: What share of the 1843 paper consisted of Lovelace’s own notes?

questions.stem: Which of the following statements would Lovelace most likely agree with?

options.A: A machine could make music only if people first turned musical rules into a form it could follow.
options.B: A machine that could compose music would also be able to come up with new ideas entirely of its own.
options.C: Music is too much like poetry to be handled by a machine that was built for arithmetic.
options.D: The engine was valuable mainly because it could calculate the Bernoulli numbers.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the events in Oxford in 2015?

options.A: To show that Turing was right to reject Lovelace’s view of the engine.
options.B: To show that the Analytical Engine was finally built 200 years after her birth.
options.C: To show that her link between the engine and music was later explored.
options.D: To show that her musical ideas were tried out while she was still alive.

translation_zh.text:
1843 年，一位年輕的數學家提出：機器也許有一天能夠作曲。她的想法之所以了不起，在於她心中的那台機器只存在於紙上。
愛達‧勒芙蕾絲生於 1815 年，是詩人拜倫勳爵唯一的孩子。她的母親讓她學習數學與科學，部分原因是希望讓她遠離父親那種詩人的性情。勒芙蕾絲從未上過學校或大學，但她從小用功，後來還透過書信跟數學家奧古斯都‧德摩根修習數學課程。即使如此，這位詩人的女兒並沒有放棄想像力；她把自己的思考方式稱為「詩意的科學」。
她的機會來自查爾斯‧巴貝奇。巴貝奇從 1830 年代中期起就在設計一台名為「分析機」的計算機器。這台機器要用打孔卡來控制，就像引導雅卡爾織布機織出圖案的那種卡片。1842 年，義大利工程師路易吉‧梅納布雷亞用法文發表了一篇介紹這台機器的文章，勒芙蕾絲受託把它譯成英文。巴貝奇建議她加上自己的注解。這篇論文在 1843 年刊出時只署了她的姓名縮寫，而在全文 66 頁中，她的注解就占了 41 頁。最後一則注解 Note G 說明了這台機器如何計算一組叫做白努利數的數列，其中的表格常被稱為世界上第一個電腦程式。
然而，她最大膽的想法和算術關係不大。巴貝奇主要把他的機器看成處理數字的工具，但勒芙蕾絲注意到，告訴機器該做什麼的卡片，和機器處理的數值是分開的。那麼在原則上，凡是遵守數學規則的東西，它都能處理。她推論：如果音與音之間的關係能用這樣的形式表達，這台機器就可能創作出任何長度、任何複雜程度的樂曲。
不過，她也小心不把話說得太滿。她寫道，這台機器不能自己創造出任何東西，只能執行人們知道如何命令它去做的事。後來艾倫‧圖靈挑戰了這個看法，並稱之為「勒芙蕾絲夫人的反對意見」。這台機器本身從未建造出來；但在 2015 年，牛津舉辦紀念她誕生 200 週年的活動時，有人用電腦模擬這台機器產生一串數字，再把它變成一段音樂主題。

open_tasks.prompt: Lovelace believed that a machine can only do what people know how to order it to do. Do you think this is still true of computers today? Answer in 1–2 English sentences and give one reason.
reference_answers: I think it is mostly still true, because even a computer that writes music follows rules and data that people have given it.
I don’t fully agree, because some computer programs today can produce results that their makers did not plan or predict.

problems: 第二段「Ada Lovelace, born in 1815, was the poet Lord Byron’s only child.」與事實單 f1 不符：f1 與來源 Bodleian（s1）都寫她是拜倫「與妻子 Anne Isabella」唯一的孩子；拜倫另有非婚生女兒 Allegra（1817–1822），寫成「拜倫唯一的孩子」是事實錯誤（中譯「詩人拜倫勳爵唯一的孩子」同樣錯）。這是選文本身的錯，不能用註解小修處理；重生時改寫為 the only child of the poet Lord Byron and his wife（或 Lord Byron’s only legitimate child）
